entries.notes: H1 correction (Marcus Reed): this entry was wrongly raised to blast yellow at G4(d) on a misreading of -Q as clock-stepping (Caleb Stone's CR-T-34 note read -Q for -q; Eli Cross's ruling and this branch's previous commit both repeated it). chronyd(8) draws a clear line between the two: -q is the mode that actually adjusts the system time and then quits (content-src/raw/rhel8/chronyd.man.txt#L64-L66, identical at rhel10#L64-L66); -Q behaves the same way except for that one adjustment -- it reports the measured offset and, because it skips opening network ports entirely, can run as a non-root user as long as nothing in the config needs elevated access (#L68-L74, identical at rhel10#L68-L74). This toolkit only ever generates -Q. blast restored to green. MCR-SEC-025: chronyd(8) SYNOPSIS is `chronyd [OPTION]... [DIRECTIVE]...` (#L7, identical at rhel10#L7), so configuration directives are OPERANDS accepted after the options, and -Q itself takes no argument (#L68). The directive is a separate word after -Q, never -Q's value. RHEL 7 uses chronyd by default for NTP (chrony package). The legacy ntpd daemon is available as an alternative from the separate ntp package but is not installed or enabled by default on any pinned release (RHEL 7 System Administrator's Guide, ch. 18-19) -- chronyd is the only NTP daemon this toolkit generates commands for.
